title: A linear model's out-of-fold disagreement finds flipped labels: most dropped samples are mislabeled, and refitting recovers much of the lost accuracy
storyline: Label noise costs a linear classifier much of its accuracy, and the usual repairs need a clean validation set or an estimate of the noise rate. We start from a measurement: when a cross-validated logistic regression disagrees with a training label on data it was not fit on, that label is usually flipped, and this disagreement catches most of the flipped labels at 20% and 40% symmetric noise on two datasets. The key idea is to use that signal directly: drop every sample the out-of-fold model disagrees with and refit on the rest, which needs no clean data and no noise-rate estimate. It works because a flipped label contradicts the structure the other labels share, and out-of-fold prediction keeps the model from memorizing the very sample it judges. The filter beats logistic regression on noisy labels wherever the test is clear, wins back most of the lost accuracy on digits, beats an untuned MLP trained on the same labels in every seed, and costs no measurable accuracy on clean labels; it does not reach clean-label accuracy at 40% noise and recovers only a fifth of the loss on breast cancer at 40%. What it changes is the default: for a linear model under label noise, this cheap out-of-fold filter is the baseline any more elaborate method should be measured against.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.goal: The reader knows in one paragraph that a linear model's out-of-fold disagreement is a reliable detector of flipped labels, that dropping and refitting recovers much of the accuracy noise costs, and where it falls short.
points: One paragraph. Problem: label noise lowers the accuracy of simple classifiers, and the usual fixes need a clean validation set or a noise-rate estimate.
The measurement: when a cross-validated logistic regression disagrees with a training label, that label is usually flipped, and the disagreement catches most flipped labels.

We present out-of-fold filtering: fit logistic regression with K-fold cross-validation, drop every sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its label, refit; no clean data, no noise-rate estimate.
Evaluation breadth in general terms: two small datasets, symmetric noise up to 40%, paired seeds.

Main insight: the filter wins back most of the lost accuracy on digits, beats an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels, and costs no measurable accuracy on clean labels; it stays below clean-label accuracy at 40% noise and was not compared with other noise-robust methods. No lists of numbers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.goal: The reader believes that out-of-fold disagreement is a cheap, side-information-free signal of flipped labels, that turning it into a drop-and-refit filter recovers much of the accuracy noise costs a linear model, and that this filter is the baseline to beat.
points: The problem: labels collected at scale are often wrong, and a linear model trained on them loses accuracy (on digits, 40% symmetric noise costs logistic regression about 13 points). Repairs such as loss correction or reweighting need a noise-rate estimate or a clean validation set that practitioners often do not have.

The measurement that motivates the paper: a logistic regression that has not seen a sample, and disagrees with its label, is usually right. Point to Fig. 1a: most samples it flags are truly flipped and it flags most of the flips.

The key idea in one sentence and why it works: drop every sample the out-of-fold model disagrees with and refit. A flipped label contradicts the structure the other labels share, and out-of-fold prediction keeps the model from memorizing the sample it judges. This revisits classical cross-validated filtering of mislabeled data as a baseline that needs no side information.

What it changes, pointing to Fig. 1b and 1c: the filter wins back about two thirds or more of the accuracy lost on digits, beats an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels, and costs no measurable accuracy on clean labels. Say in one clause that it does not reach clean-label accuracy at 40% noise.

Contribution list, three bullets each starting with a verb: (1) We show that out-of-fold disagreement of a logistic regression with a training label is a precise and high-recall detector of flipped labels on two datasets at 20% and 40% symmetric noise. (2) We propose a filter that drops every disagreeing sample and refits, needing no clean validation set and no noise-rate estimate. (3) We show that it improves over logistic regression and over an untuned MLP on the same noisy labels, costs little on clean labels, and we report where it falls short.

sections.title: Related work
sections.goal: The reader places the filter among noisy-label methods: it is the simplest member of the sample-selection family, needs less side information than correction methods, and was not compared with co-teaching or confident learning.
points: Learning with noisy labels (bold run-in): surveys organize the field into robust losses, loss correction, reweighting and sample selection; correction and reweighting need a noise transition estimate or a clean validation set. Ends: our filter needs neither.

Sample selection and confident learning (bold run-in): co-teaching selects small-loss samples with two networks and needs the noise rate to set how many to keep; confident learning uses out-of-sample predicted probabilities and per-class thresholds to estimate the joint noise distribution and prune. Ends: we keep only the argmax-disagreement rule of a linear model, with no threshold and no rate, and we did not run these methods, so we make no claim against them.

Filtering mislabeled training data (bold run-in): classical work removes samples that cross-validated classifiers misclassify. Ends: we revisit this rule for a linear model, measure its precision and recall against known flips, and measure what refitting buys against the noisy model and a larger one.

sections.title: Out-of-fold filtering for label noise
sections.goal: The reader can implement the filter from one paragraph and sees why out-of-fold disagreement singles out flipped labels without any side information.
points: Setting and notation, defined once: a training set of n samples x_i with observed, possibly flipped labels ỹ_i; a classifier f (logistic regression on standardized features). The filter is a function from the noisy training set to a refit classifier.

The rule, introduced in words before the equations: split the training set into K stratified folds; for each sample, predict its label with the model fit on the other K-1 folds (out-of-fold prediction ŷ_i); keep the set S of samples where ŷ_i equals ỹ_i; refit f on S. Fig. 2 shows the four steps. We use K = 5 and C = 1.

Why it works: a flipped label disagrees with the decision boundary the other, mostly correct labels define, so a model that never saw the sample tends to predict its true class; fitting on the sample itself would let the model bend toward the wrong label, which out-of-fold prediction prevents.
What it does not need: no clean validation set, no noise-rate estimate, no threshold on confidence; the only setting is K. The cost is K + 1 fits of a linear model.

sections.title: Experimental setup
sections.goal: The reader knows exactly what was run, how the comparisons are tested, and the scope of the study, in one compact paragraph block.
points: Data and noise: two small scikit-learn datasets, digits (10 classes) and breast cancer (2 classes), split 70/30 with stratification per seed (train and test sizes). Symmetric noise flips each training label with probability 0%, 20% or 40% to a uniformly drawn other class; the sampled flip rate at nominal 40% is slightly below nominal. Test labels stay clean.

Methods: logistic regression trained on the noisy labels (also the no-filter ablation), an MLP with one hidden layer of 64 units and scikit-learn defaults for up to 500 iterations (untuned), and the filter. Logistic regression on clean labels (0% noise) is the reference for recovered accuracy; no oracle run exists. Co-teaching and confident learning were not run.

Metrics: test accuracy on clean labels; precision of the drop set (share of dropped samples that were truly flipped) and recall (share of flipped labels dropped); recovered share = (filter minus noisy logistic regression) / (clean minus noisy logistic regression), computed from 5-seed means.

Statistics: 5 seeds paired across methods (shared split and noise draw), 90 runs in total; paired t-tests and 95% intervals of paired differences; tables report mean ± sd. No hyperparameter was tuned.

sections.title: Results
sections.goal: The reader sees, in four findings, that disagreement detects flipped labels, that refitting recovers most of the loss on digits and part of it on breast cancer, that the filter beats an untuned MLP under noise, and that it costs no measurable accuracy on clean labels.
points: Subsection 'Out-of-fold disagreement flags flipped labels with high precision and recall'. Insight first: in every noisy cell most dropped samples are truly flipped (precision above 50% with p < 0.001 per cell; even the worst single run stays above 60%), and the filter drops most flipped labels, nearly all of them on digits (Table 2, Fig. 1a). The price is visible in the same table: a quarter to a third of the dropped samples are clean.

Subsection 'Refitting on the kept samples recovers most of the lost accuracy on digits', paragraph 1: noise hurts logistic regression on both datasets (13 and 16 points at 40%, Table 1). The filter beats it on digits at both rates and on breast cancer at 40%, with paired intervals that exclude zero (Table 1). On digits it wins back about 78% of the loss at 20% noise and 68% at 40%.

Same subsection, paragraph 2, the limits stated plainly: on breast cancer the filter recovers about two thirds at 20% but only about a fifth at 40%, where the seed variance is large; the 3-point gain at 20% is not significant with 5 seeds. At 40% noise the filter stays below clean-label accuracy on both datasets (paired tests against the clean model). Recovered shares are ratios of means because per-seed ratios are unstable when the loss is small.

Subsection 'The filter beats an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels': the filter wins in all 5 seeds of every noisy cell, by 11 to 28 points, with intervals far from zero (Table 3, Fig. 1b). The MLP fits the flipped labels and falls to about 65% at 40% noise on both datasets, faster than the linear model; state this as an observed trend for one untuned MLP, with no test on its own trend.

Subsection 'On clean labels the filter costs little': the change against logistic regression is a fraction of a point on both datasets and not significant, with 95% intervals that include zero (Table 1, Fig. 1c), although the filter still drops 3.5% (digits) and 1.9% (breast cancer) of clean training samples. On clean digits the MLP is ahead of the filter by about 0.7 points; on clean breast cancer the two are level (no difference detected).

sections.title: Discussion and limitations
sections.goal: The reader takes away that out-of-fold filtering should be the default baseline for a linear model under label noise, and knows the specific limits that future work should test.
points: Big picture: a linear model's disagreement on held-out folds is enough to find most flipped labels, and acting on it is cheap; for linear models under label noise, this filter is the baseline more elaborate methods should report against.

Limitations framed as directions: the filter also discards clean samples (a quarter to a third of drops), recovers only a fifth of the loss on breast cancer at 40% noise, and stays below clean-label accuracy at 40% noise; a softer rule (confidence thresholds, reweighting instead of dropping) or a second filtering round may close the gap.

Scope: two small datasets, symmetric noise up to 40%, 5 seeds, one K and C, one untuned MLP, and no comparison with co-teaching or confident learning; class-dependent noise, larger data and those comparisons are the next experiments. The filter is about 5 times slower to fit than plain logistic regression on digits, still faster than the MLP (single timing on one machine). No claim about deep networks or large data.

figures.message: When the out-of-fold logistic regression disagrees with a label, the label is usually flipped; dropping those samples closes much of the accuracy gap that noise opens (especially on digits) while the MLP falls away, and on clean labels the filter costs nothing measurable.
figures.spec: Three panels side by side, digits and breast cancer distinguished consistently (two rows or hatching/marker per dataset). (a) The measurement: grouped bars of precision (share of dropped samples truly flipped) and recall (share of flipped labels dropped) at 20% and 40% noise for both datasets, filter color #4E2A84 for precision and light purple #B6ACD1 for recall, individual seed points overlaid, error bars sd over 5 seeds, dashed horizontal line at 50% labeled 'half of drops'. (b) The consequence: test accuracy (%) against noise rate (0, 20, 40%) for logistic regression (one muted colorblind-safe hue, e.g. teal), the MLP (a second muted hue, e.g. orange-brown) and the filter (#4E2A84), mean ± sd over 5 seeds, with the clean-label logistic regression accuracy as a gray horizontal reference line per dataset; shade or bracket the gap the filter closes. (c) The price on clean labels: small bars of the paired accuracy change filter minus logistic regression at 0% noise for each dataset with 95% interval error bars crossing zero, and next to it the share (%) of clean training samples dropped. Sans-serif regular labels, axes with units, legends off the data, no titles inside panels.
figures.caption: Out-of-fold disagreement finds flipped labels, and dropping them recovers much of the accuracy that label noise costs a linear model. (a) Precision and recall of the samples the filter drops at 20% and 40% symmetric noise; dots are seeds, error bars are sd over 5 seeds, and the dashed line marks 50%. Most dropped samples are truly flipped, and most flipped labels are dropped. (b) Test accuracy of logistic regression and an untuned MLP trained on the noisy labels and of the filter; the gray line is logistic regression on clean labels. The filter closes much of the gap on digits, while the MLP falls fastest. (c) On clean labels, the accuracy change of the filter against logistic regression (95% intervals over 5 paired seeds) includes zero, at the price of dropping a few percent of clean samples.

figures.message: The filter is four steps: split the noisy training set into folds, predict each sample with a model that never saw it, drop the samples whose prediction disagrees with the label, and refit on the rest.
figures.spec: Left-to-right flow of four flat pastel rounded panels marked with small numbered circles: (1) 'Noisy labels': a small grid of sample icons with colored labels, a few with a red-orange mismatched tag; (2) 'Out-of-fold predict': the grid split into 5 fold strips, a network card in #4E2A84 fit on 4 strips and predicting the fifth; (3) 'Drop disagreements': samples whose predicted class differs from the label crossed out; (4) 'Refit': a logistic regression card in #4E2A84 trained on the kept samples. Thick rounded arrows between panels, lavender #F1EEF7 backgrounds, one to three word labels, no equations, sans-serif regular font.
figures.caption: Out-of-fold filtering. (1) The training labels contain flips. (2) Logistic regression is fit with K-fold cross-validation, so each sample is predicted by a model that did not see it. (3) Every sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its given label is dropped. (4) Logistic regression is refit on the kept samples. The filter uses no clean validation set and no estimate of the noise rate; we use K = 5.
